“The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on economic activity in the near term and pose risks to the economic outlook.” In line with the literature on monetary transmission and crisis policy, the FOMC’s swift move to the effective lower bound and large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, along with expanded repos and discount-window access, are aimed at stabilizing funding markets and lowering risk premia. Credit-channel research (Bernanke-Gertler; Gertler and Gilchrist; Oliner and Rudebusch; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein) indicates such measures can reduce the external finance premium, supporting business fixed investment and employment—especially for smaller, bank-dependent firms. With market- and survey-based inflation expectations soft and inflation below 2 percent, New Keynesian models and inflation-forecast targeting (Svensson) suggest forceful accommodation helps close the output gap without unanchoring inflation expectations. Given zero lower bound and liquidity-trap risks (e.g., Eichenbaum-Fuerst liquidity effects), balance-sheet policies and globally coordinated dollar swap lines are appropriate open-economy tools to ease dollar funding strains and support credit flow. Net tone: still negative near term due to the COVID-19 shock and market dysfunction, but partially offset by credible, aggressive policy actions that the literature associates with mitigating real-economy declines.
